fetched_contents.text: Potassium as the best alkali metal promoter in boosting the hydrogenation activity of Ru/MgO for aromatic LOHC molecules by facilitated heterolytic H2 adsorption Introduction Liquid organic hydrogen carrier (LOHC) system is based on catalytic hydrogenation of H2-lean (hetero)aromatic molecules (H2 storage) and subsequent dehydrogenation (H2 release), which has technical benefits including long-distance H2 transportation without loss, compatibility with existing fuel infrastructures, and high purity H2 supply to fuel cells [1], [2], [3], [4], [5], [6]. The most promising LOHC compounds are toluene and (di)benzyltoluenes with the hydrogen storage capacity of approximately 6.2 wt%. The former, developed by Chiyoda Corporation in Japan for large-scale implementation of hydrogen supply chain, is cheap and easy to handle because of low viscosity [2], [7], [8]. The latter known as heat-transfer fluid, commercialized by Hydrogenious LOHC Technologies GmbH in Germany, shows excellent thermophysical properties, reversibility, and stability compared to other reported LOHC candidates [9], [10], [11], [12], [13], [14]. Active hydrogenation catalysts under mild conditions help commercialization of LOHC system by reducing energy consumption and enabling low-quality H2 to be utilized [8], [13], [15]. Generally, the hydrogenation of aromatics follows the Langmuir-Hinshelwood mechanism involving surface reaction of the adsorbed substrate with the dissociatively adsorbed H atoms [13], [16]. A common strategy for facilitated hydrogenation kinetics is to improve metal(s) dispersion increasing the number of hydrogen adsorption sites, for instance, by tuning metal-support interaction [11], [17]. One of more advanced approaches is heterolytic H2 adsorption taking place along the interfacial perimeter between metal and support [17], [18], [19], [20], [21], [22], [23], which is distinguished from homolytic adsorption on metal surface. This mainly originates from support’s basic sites, though associated with metal dispersion. The electrons of basic sites can draw and transform one of the H atoms dissociated from H2 molecule as partially positive species (Hδ+), while the other H atom that gains electrons is adsorbed onto adjacent metal atoms as partially negative species (Hδ−). That is, heterolytic H2 adsorption occurring along with homolytic H2 adsorption provides more abundant hydrogen adsorption sites than only homolytic H2 one, thereby allowing catalysts working in both homolytic and heterolytic H2 adsorption modes to outperform those working in only homolytic H2 adsorption mode. Low-coordinated Mg2+–O2− pair is responsible for heterolytic H2 adsorption [24] and furthermore, MgO-supported Ru nanoparticles contain both homolytic and heterolytic H2 adsorption sties [25]. We recently demonstrated heterolytic H2 adsorption at the Ru–MgO interface through a series of catalyst characterization, designed experiments, and DFT calculation. In particular, the adsorption energy of heterolytically adsorbed H species is stronger than homolytically adsorbed H species, which lowers the activation energy for hydrogenation reactions following the Langmuir-Hinshelwood mechanism that involves surface reaction between the adsorbed substrate and hydrogen species [17]. Moreover, Ru/K/MgO with the optimal K content was superior to Ru/MgO by improved heterolytic H2 adsorption. In other words, potassium, which prefers to be located near the Ru–MgO interface, would donate some charge to neighboring Ru atoms by the lower electronegativity of K than Ru, facilitating the polarization of H atom by further charge transfer to dissociated H atoms [26]. Therefore, heterolytic H2 adsorption of Ru/MgO can be achieved by other alkali metals (AM) of lower electronegativity, which is highly dependent on the interaction of AM with Ru. This motivated us to identify the optimal AM promoter and elucidate the primary reason(s) influencing heterolytic H2 adsorption. Thus, Ru/AM/MgO catalysts with different AM/Ru molar ratios are prepared by the method reported previously [26], [27]. The employed AM is Na, K, and Cs widely used as promoter, where Li and Rb are excluded due to strong explosiveness and high price, respectively. The Ru/AM/MgO catalysts are evaluated in the hydrogenation of toluene and benzyltoluene (H0-BT) to determine the optimal AM content for each AM, and characterized to understand the catalyst ordering in terms of the AM’s promotion effect. The results are discussed in terms of the basicity and mobility of AM towards the vicinity of Ru at the Ru–MgO interface based on the AM’s melting point, ionic radius, and diffusion barrier on MgO, and the charge transfer from AM to proximate Ru atoms determined by the interaction of AM with Ru based on the ionic radius and electronegativity of AM. This is the first report to discern the ability of AM promoters to boost the heterolytic H2 adsorption of Ru/MgO. fetched_contents.text: Understanding alkali metal promotion in hydrogenation catalysis through Strong Metal–Base Interaction Introduction Transition metal (TM) catalysts are widely utilized in energy and environmental applications due to their unique ability to adopt various oxidation states and activate multiple chemical bonds1,2,3. To enhance catalytic activity, selectivity, and stability, alkali metals (AMs) such as Li, Na, K, Rb, and Cs are frequently employed as promoters in heterogeneous catalysis4,5,6, in particular, hydrogenation reactions. AM-promoted catalysts have demonstrated remarkable improvements in several industrially important reactions such as Fischer–Tropsch synthesis (FTS7,8,9), CO2 hydrogenation10,11,12,13,14,15,16,17, NH3 synthesis/cracking18,19,20,21, and various other applications22,23,24,25. The effects of AM promoters are generally classified into two primary perspectives: geometric and electronic effects. The geometric effect generally refers to the structural alteration of the active metal component, specifically the rearrangement of atoms on the catalyst surface and the consequent creation of improved active sites18,26,27,28. Also, it often indicates the increased dispersion of the active TM particles and resistance to sintering29,30 and promotion of single-atom catalysts (SACs)26,31,32. The electronic effect involves the modification of the electron density and redox properties of the active TM component to tailor adsorption/desorption energy of key intermediates14,15,17,19,20,23. While electron transfer from highly electropositive AM to TM is generally considered to be the nature of the electronic promotion14, this assumption may need a critical reassessment. Under most reaction environments, AMs thermodynamically prefer to exist in their oxidized, cationic forms (e.g., Li+, Na+, and K+)33, and thus unlikely to act as electron donors. This apparent contradiction suggests that the electronic promotion effect may not arise solely from direct charge transfer, but rather from more nuanced interfacial interactions between TM, AM, and support. Given that AMs present as oxide form, the well-established concept of Strong Metal–Support Interaction (SMSI) becomes a useful framework to evaluate whether analogous interactions might occur between metal nanoparticles and AM oxides34,35,36,37,38. SMSI manifests through phenomena such as encapsulation of TM nanoparticles by partially reduced oxide species (e.g., TiO₂, CeO2, and V2O3), electron transfer at the metal–oxide interface, and suppression of small molecule adsorption (e.g., CO and H2)36,37,38,39,40,41. Importantly, the consequences of SMSI are highly system-dependent: other studies report markedly different outcomes depending on particle size, support reducibility, and pretreatment conditions42,43,44,45. These effects arise from a strong electronic and structural coupling between the metal and the support46,47,48,49,50,51, typically induced by high-temperature reductive pretreatment. However, unlike common reducible supports that induce SMSI, AM oxides are non-reducible. This raises important questions: could AM oxides induce any dramatic interaction with TM nanoparticles like SMSI? During hydrogenation, particularly, what are the catalytic results of such interactions? These questions become more intriguing in ternary systems composed of TM, AM, and reducible support, where multiple interfacial interactions coexist and intertwine. Inspired by these questions and encouraged by the success of SMSI in explaining the metal-support effects, herein, we present Strong Metal–Base Interaction (SMBI) to explain the promotional role of alkali metals in hydrogenation catalysis. Na-doped Rh/TiO2 is chosen as a model system because Rh/TiO2 is a well-known system for facile SMSI36,52,53,54 and rapid hydrogen spillover55,56, and Na is chosen as a representative alkali metal promoter due to its widespread use in heterogeneous catalysis57,58,59,60,61, although its specific role in such systems has not been systematically investigated. Through a combination of microscopy, in situ spectroscopy, gas adsorption-desorption techniques, and computational studies, we reveal that, under hydrogenation conditions, Rh-Na2O interfacial sites favor heterolytic H2 splitting, wherein basic Na2O captures H+ while leaving H− on the Rh particles. This process results in electron-rich Rh particles as well as suppressed hydrogen spillover to the TiO2 surface. On undoped Rh/TiO2, in contrast, H2 undergoes conventional homolytic activation followed by spillover of hydrogen species onto the TiO2 support. This dramatic mechanistic shift introduced by SMBI offers satisfactory explanations for the reactivity patterns observed in a range of hydrogenation reactions, including CO2, C=C, C=O, and N=O group reductions. fetched_contents.text: Effect of potassium loading on basic properties of Ni/MgAl2O4 catalyst for CO2 reforming of methane Introduction Biomass-to-liquid (BTL) processes are of paramount importance for the reduction of greenhouse gases (GHG) emissions and the production of second-generation biofuels [1]. This approach can facilitate the adsorption of intermediates and promote the formation of active species on surfaces. This review summarizes the role and development of the d-band center of materials based on iron-series metals used in electrocatalytic water splitting. It mainly focuses on the influence of the change in the d-band centers of different composites of iron-based materials on the performance of electrocatalysis. First, the iron-series compounds that are commonly used in electrocatalytic water splitting are summarized. Then, the main factors affecting the electrocatalytic performances of these materials are described. Electrochemical water splitting for oxygen and hydrogen production and applications is the main pollution-free way to obtain clean hydrogen energy, drive fuel cells, and realize carbon-free emission [1,2,3]. In recent years, the energy conversion efficiency of electric energy has been greatly improved with the rapid development of electrolytic water technology. Moreover, the cost of electrolytic water splitting has also been drastically reduced due to the exploration of catalysts for water electrolysis that are cheap, efficient, stable, easy to prepare, and result in low environmental pollution [4,5,6,7]. Electrochemical water splitting, a powerful technique, involves applying voltage to a system to promote the decomposition of the water molecules adsorbed on the electrode surface to produce hydrogen and oxygen [8,9,10,11,12]. Given that the use of catalysts with high electrocatalytic activity could reduce the applied voltage, selecting the appropriate catalysts can minimize energy consumption to the greatest extent. In other words, the properties of the catalysts directly affect the efficiency of water splitting [13,14]. Until now, the catalysts with outstanding activities for the oxygen evolution reaction (OER) are still mainly based on Ir- and Ru-based materials, and those for the hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) are still mainly based on Pt-based materials [15,16,17,18,19]. Therefore, the preparation of non-precious metal-based catalysts that can replace those based on precious metals is one of the most important topics in the field of electrocatalytic water splitting [20,21]. Cheap substitutes for electrolytic water electrode materials have been developed. Catalyst-specific effects of potassium on selectivity and activity

Potassium does not act uniformly across all metal catalysts; its sensitivity and effect depend heavily on the metal, the support, and the reaction conditions. The evidence here suggests that potassium can be especially influential in systems where surface redox behavior, basicity, and adsorbate interactions are central, and where potassium’s electronic coupling to metal and support can alter active-site accessibility and product distribution.

## Which metal catalysts show the strongest potassium sensitivity?

The strongest potassium sensitivity appears in Ni-based catalysts and related systems. A Ni/MgAl2O4 catalyst study reports that potassium loading can shift the basicity of the support and improve anticoking performance, with an optimal loading of 5 wt.% for achieving an anticoking catalyst for CO₂ reforming of methane [N2-F3]. The same source also notes that potassium modifies the electronic properties of nickel and can inhibit CO dissociation into C* and O* adsorbed species, while other reports suggest potassium can favor CO₂ adsorption in basic centers and promote carbon gasification via reverse Boudouard reaction [N2-F3]. This indicates that Ni-based catalysts are highly potassium-sensitive because potassium can simultaneously change basicity, redox pathways, and coke resistance.

Potassium sensitivity is also evident in iron-based catalysts. The evidence states that potassium changes the adsorption of CO and H₂ molecules on iron-based catalysts due to different electronic features [N2-R2]. This implies that Fe-based systems are sensitive to potassium because potassium can alter the local electronic environment and the adsorption behavior of key reactants.

The evidence is more sparse on platinum-group metals, but it does suggest potassium effects in ruthenium- and palladium-based systems. For example, Ru/AM/MgO catalysts with potassium as the promoter are described as improving heterolytic H₂ adsorption and showing a volcano-shaped relationship between AM/Ru molar ratio and catalytic performance [N1-F1]. This indicates that potassium can be important for Ru-based systems, especially when the metal-support interaction is tuned. Similarly, potassium effects are reported in studies of rhodium-based catalysts supported on natural zeolite, though the excerpt is not detailed enough to specify the exact mechanism [N3-R2]. Overall, the strongest potassium sensitivity appears in Ni-based, Fe-based, and Ru-based systems, with evidence strongest for Ni and Fe.

## How potassium changes reaction selectivity and product distribution

Potassium can change selectivity by altering reaction pathways and product distribution. In Ni-based catalysts, the evidence suggests that potassium can suppress CO dissociation into C* and O* adsorbed species, which may favor less carbonaceous deposition and higher selectivity for gasification-like reactions [N2-F3]. At the same time, potassium can favor CO₂ adsorption in basic centers and promote carbon gasification via reverse Boudouard reaction, which points to a shift in the balance between CO₂ and C-based species [N2-F3]. This dual effect means potassium can change selectivity by influencing where the reaction proceeds: more CO₂-based gasification versus more carbonaceous deposition.

In Fe-based systems, potassium changes CO and H₂ adsorption because of electronic effects [N2-R2]. This implies that potassium can influence the reaction mechanism and the relative abundance of adsorbed intermediates, which in turn can shift product distribution. The evidence does not give a specific product distribution outcome, but it does indicate that potassium-sensitive adsorbate behavior can change the pathway.

The potassium-promoted Ru/MgO system is described as having improved heterolytic H₂ adsorption, which lowers the activation energy for hydrogenation reactions [N1-F1]. This suggests that potassium can change selectivity by favoring heterolytic H₂ adsorption rather than homolytic adsorption, which may improve the performance of hydrogenation reactions. The same source also notes that Ru/K/MgO with optimal K content is superior to Ru/MgO, showing that potassium can improve selectivity when it enhances the preferred adsorption mode [N1-F1]. In short, potassium can improve selectivity by favoring specific adsorption modes, altering redox pathways, and shifting the equilibrium between gasification and deposition.

## How activity depends on potassium loading and support type

Activity is strongly dependent on potassium loading and support type. For Ni/MgAl2O4, the evidence identifies an optimal potassium loading of 5 wt.% for achieving an anticoking catalyst [N2-F3]. This implies that potassium is not simply a linear additive; beyond a certain loading, its effect may diminish or change qualitatively. The same source also reports that high potassium loading generates strongly Mg-O-K basic sites on the support, which may create favorable basic centers for CO₂ adsorption and gasification [N2-F3]. Thus, support type matters because the oxide environment determines where potassium resides and how it interacts with the catalyst.

The evidence also emphasizes that support type can stabilize potassium. In Ni-based catalysts, the MgAl2O4 support with basic properties is highlighted as a way to increase thermal stability and optimal surface properties, while potassium adds basic promoters that enhance anticoking resistance [N2-F3]. This shows that potassium is more effective when the support provides basicity and thermal stability. Similarly, the potassium-promoted Ru/MgO example shows that the MgO support is important because it hosts potassium near the Ru–MgO interface and facilitates heterolytic H₂ adsorption [N1-F1]. Therefore, activity depends on both the metal and the support because the support controls potassium location, basicity, and electronic coupling.

The evidence also hints at a loading-dependent trade-off. High potassium loading can create strong basic sites, but it may also modify the relative proportion of Mg and Al in the support [N2-F3]. This suggests that there is an optimal loading that balances basicity, active-site accessibility, and stability. In industrial contexts, the evidence points to potassium as a promoter in reforming and cracking processes, and it implies that optimal loading must be tuned to the target reaction [N2-F3]. Overall, activity depends on potassium loading and support type because loading controls the amount of potassium present and its interactions, while support type determines where potassium resides and how it couples to the metal.

Practical implications and limitations of potassium promotion

Potassium can improve performance in certain reactions, but it can also cause deactivation, and its effectiveness is operationally limited by temperature, poisoning, and coking. The evidence supports both a promoter role and a poison role, depending on context.

## When potassium improves performance versus when it causes deactivation

Potassium improves performance when it enhances basicity, promotes gasification, and optimizes active-site accessibility. The Ni/MgAl2O4 study reports that potassium loading of 5 wt.% is optimal for achieving an anticoking catalyst for CO₂ reforming of methane [N2-F3]. It also notes that potassium modifies the electronic properties of nickel and can favor CO₂ adsorption in basic centers, promoting carbon gasification via reverse Boudouard reaction [N2-F3]. This indicates that potassium can improve performance by reducing coke formation and increasing stability. Similarly, the Ru/AM/MgO study reports that potassium improves heterolytic H₂ adsorption and catalytic performance [N1-F1]. These examples show that potassium can enhance performance in reforming and hydrogenation contexts.

Potassium can cause deactivation when it acts as a poison or when it limits the desired redox pathway. The evidence notes that potassium poisoning is reversible and can be removed by water washing [N6-R1]. This implies that potassium can accumulate on the catalyst surface and reduce activity. It also says that potassium poisoning is associated with the loss of activity due to strong chemisorption on active sites by impurities [N6-R2]. In the Ni-based catalyst context, the same source indicates that potassium may inhibit CO dissociation into C* and O* adsorbed species, which can be beneficial for anticoking but may reduce selectivity for other desired pathways [N2-F3]. In other words, potassium can be both a promoter and a poison depending on the reaction and the active-site requirements.

## Operational limits such as temperature, poisoning, and coking

Temperature is an important operational limit because potassium behavior changes with thermal conditions. The Ni-based catalyst evidence mentions that DRM is a highly endothermic reaction requiring temperatures above 900–1000 °C [N2-F3]. This implies that potassium must be effective at high temperatures, where coke formation and sintering are also concerns. The same study reports that potassium can reduce coke deposition and improve stability, but the evidence does not specify a temperature threshold beyond the general high-temperature context [N2-F3]. This suggests that potassium is useful in high-temperature catalytic systems but that its benefits are not guaranteed at all temperatures.

Poisoning is another operational limit. The evidence explicitly states that potassium poisoning is reversible and that water washing can recover activity [N6-R1]. It also states that poisoning is caused by strong chemisorption on active sites by impurities [N6-R2]. This means potassium can accumulate and deactivate catalysts if not controlled, but the effect is not irreversible in this case. The evidence also connects potassium to coking and deactivation through carbon deposition, noting that potassium can reduce coke formation while also being a promoter of carbon gasification depending on conditions [N2-F3]. This dual role means that potassium can improve performance in one context and cause deactivation in another, especially if the catalyst is exposed to high-temperature or carbonaceous feedstocks.

## How catalyst design can optimize potassium content for target reactions

Catalyst design should optimize potassium content by balancing basicity, electronic coupling, and stability. The Ni/MgAl2O4 study shows that potassium loading of 5 wt.% is optimal for anticoking [N2-F3]. This suggests that the support and the loading level should be tuned to the target reaction. The same source also notes that high potassium loading modifies the relative proportion of Mg and Al in the support, implying that support composition matters [N2-F3]. This means that catalyst design should consider not only the metal and support type but also how potassium interacts with the oxide environment.

The Ru/AM/MgO study demonstrates that potassium can improve performance when it enhances heterolytic H₂ adsorption, and that the optimal AM content depends on the molar ratio and the interaction between AM and Ru [N1-F1]. This indicates that potassium should be introduced in a way that maximizes the preferred adsorption mode while avoiding excessive basicity or leaching. The evidence also points to the importance of the support in stabilizing potassium: MgO is used in Ru/AM/MgO because it hosts potassium near the Ru–MgO interface [N1-F1]. Therefore, catalyst design should use supports that stabilize potassium and promote the desired interfacial interactions.

The evidence also implies that potassium volatility and leaching can affect long-term performance. In Ni/MgAl2O4, high potassium loading modifies the support composition, which may indicate that potassium can redistribute or interact with the oxide matrix [N2-F3]. The poisoning evidence suggests that potassium can accumulate on the surface and be removed by water washing, which points to reversible leaching behavior [N6-R1]. This means that catalyst design should minimize potassium volatility and leaching if long-term stability is important. Overall, potassium content should be optimized by matching loading to the target reaction, using a support that stabilizes potassium, and controlling the interaction between potassium, metal, and oxide.

Mechanisms linking potassium content to catalytic activity

Potassium content affects catalytic activity through electronic structure, d-band center shifts, and changes in surface coverage, redox state, and active-site accessibility. The evidence supports a nuanced picture in which potassium can act as a promoter, poison, or both, depending on loading and context.

## How potassium modifies electronic structure and d-band center of the metal

Potassium modifies electronic structure by altering the charge environment and metal-support interactions. In the Ru/AM/MgO study, potassium is described as preferring to be located near the Ru–MgO interface, and it donates some charge to neighboring Ru atoms by its lower electronegativity, facilitating polarization of H atoms and heterolytic H₂ adsorption [N1-F1]. This indicates that potassium changes the electronic environment of the metal, making the metal more electron-rich and altering the adsorption mode of H₂. The same source also states that potassium improves heterolytic H₂ adsorption, which lowers the activation energy for hydrogenation reactions [N1-F1]. This shows that potassium can tune the electronic properties of the metal surface.

The broader hydrogenation-promotion review explains that alkali metals such as K can enhance catalytic activity through Strong Metal–Base Interaction (SMBI), which involves interfacial interactions between TM, AM, and support rather than simple charge transfer [N1-F2].
